messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
When Somchai first describes the day of the chemical exposure, he does not tell it as a distant story. At 60, after years of managing a busy American hotel, he still speaks about it as if he has stepped back into the air of that afternoon. A maintenance problem had led to cleaning chemicals being used in an enclosed service area near the lower level of the hotel. He remembers the sharp taste in his mouth almost immediately, harsh and artificial, and the sense that the air had turned against him before he fully understood what was happening. He could not simply walk away at once; there were staff moving in and out, confusion about what had spilled or mixed, and a delay before anyone seemed able to say clearly whether it was safe. He recalls waiting for answers while his throat and chest felt wrong and his body seemed suddenly outside his control. What has stayed with him most is not only the exposure itself but the conviction that when something dangerous happens, he may not be able to stop it and may not even know in time how serious it is.

In the weeks afterward, the memory did not settle into the past. It came into his mind without warning while he was at the front desk, in the service elevator, or driving home. When it returned, it did not feel like remembering. He would be back there, tasting the same bitter chemical tang on his tongue, his body tightening as if the exposure were happening again in that exact moment. Sometimes a smell in a corridor or the sight of housekeeping carts and supply bottles was enough to bring it on, but at other times the memory forced its way in without any obvious cue. He found this especially frightening because it seemed to confirm what he had come to believe: that he could no longer trust his own body. If his mouth could suddenly fill with that taste again, if his chest could tighten and his muscles brace before he had chosen to think about anything, then his body no longer felt like something dependable.

At work, these experiences became woven into his day. As hotel manager, he was expected to circulate constantly through guest floors, back offices, loading areas, laundry spaces, and maintenance corridors. Instead of moving through these spaces with the ease of habit, Somchai began scanning them. He checked the air, watched staff handling supplies, noticed whether a door to a utility room was propped open, and monitored how long someone took to respond when he asked about an odor or a delay in maintenance. If a staff member said, “We’re looking into it,” and a few minutes passed without an update, he was certain something bad might already be unfolding. A routine delay did not feel routine to him. It felt like the beginning of another situation in which danger was present while everyone was still trying to name it.

He also watched himself constantly. He paid close attention to his breathing, his throat, the feeling in his chest, any unusual taste, any small shift in how his body felt. He was trying to catch danger early, but the result was that his body rarely left a state of readiness. He described himself as always braced, shoulders tight, stomach clenched, as if preparing for something to go wrong. There were many moments when nothing was wrong at all, yet he reacted with sudden alarm, turning toward a harmless smell, a delayed phone call, or a comment from an employee about cleaning supplies as though he were under immediate threat.

Over months, he began shaping his life around not being reminded. When staff brought up the exposure, he cut the conversation short or left. He avoided going into the area where it had happened unless absolutely necessary and delegated tasks he would once have handled himself. This had consequences at work. Employees noticed that he was harder to approach and unusually preoccupied with safety checks that went beyond policy. At home, although he is in a relationship, he felt increasingly set apart. He struggled to explain why ordinary delays or offhand comments about chemical smells affected him so strongly, and he had come to feel that he no longer belonged anywhere in the easy way he once had—not fully at work, not fully at home, not even comfortably in his own body.

By the time he sought help, Somchai was exhausted by the sense of living in permanent readiness. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic collapse but the accumulation of moments in which he felt seized by the memory at work and then ashamed and alone afterward. He is frightened that this is what his life has become: a body he cannot rely on, a world where danger may already be underway whenever something takes too long, and a self who no longer fits where he used to. At the same time, he is hoping, carefully, that treatment might help him move through his hotel and his life without feeling that the air could turn dangerous again at any moment.
